analysis.one_liner: Makes large factory farms pay for disaster planning, bans cruel mass-killing methods, and adds worker and food-safety protections.
analysis.headline: Referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee in February 2023 with two Democratic cosponsors, the bill never received a hearing or vote and died when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required large industrial livestock operators to register with a new USDA office, file annual disaster plans, and pay fees covering disaster mitigation. It would have banned the cheapest mass-killing methods used to cull animals (like ventilation shutdown and sodium nitrite poisoning), with fines up to $1,000 per animal and loss of federal contracts and inspection for violators. It also would have given slaughterhouse workers and contract growers severance, health coverage, and whistleblower protections after disasters, and rolled back higher-speed slaughter lines and self-inspection rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Meat and poultry plant workers, who would get 12 weeks of severance, two years of fully paid silver-level health coverage, and whistleblower protection after disaster events. Contract growers, who would be owed lost revenue if a company canceled their contract after a disaster. People living near large feeding operations, who could sue for health and property damage. Consumers, through food-safety rules including a ban on slaughtering downed livestock and on certain growth drugs. Small and higher-welfare farmers and processors, who would get grants and extra inspection help. Farmed animals, through bans on the most painful depopulation and slaughter practices.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Meatplant workers, contract growers, rural neighbors, small farmers

how_it_helps.text: Slaughterhouse workers and contract growers hit by a disaster would get 12 weeks of severance, two years of employer-paid health coverage at silver level, whistleblower protections, and the right to sue for double damages with attorney's fees.

Large operators would have to pay all costs of a disaster or mass culling, including compensation to neighboring residents for health impacts and lost property value, instead of pushing those costs onto growers, workers, or taxpayers.

The cheapest mass-killing methods — ventilation shutdown, ventilation shutdown plus, sodium nitrite poisoning, and water-based foaming — would be banned, with civil penalties up to $1,000 per animal and a 10-year loss of federal contracts and federal inspection for violators.

The bill would end higher-speed slaughter lines and company self-inspection systems, add OSHA and federal meat inspectors, bar the slaughter and sale of nonambulatory (downed) livestock, prohibit beta-agonist growth drugs like ractopamine, and put poultry under the Humane Methods of Slaughter Act for the first time.

Small and higher-welfare processors would benefit from a $750 million grant program to switch to gas-based stunning, a pilot program adding free inspections and technical assistance, and $50 million-a-year transport research grants — a stated goal being a level playing field for farmers in a market the bill describes as highly monopolized.

analysis.who_pays: Large industrial livestock operators — those controlling 2,500 or more swine, 30,000 or more turkeys or ducks, or 82,000 or more laying hens or broilers — would pay annual registration fees of at least $1 per animal unit, bear full liability for disaster and depopulation costs including payments to neighbors, and fund severance and two years of health premiums for workers after disasters. Meatpackers would lose higher line speeds and self-inspection authority. Taxpayers would fund the $750 million stunning-transition grants and new inspector positions unless fee revenue covers them. Some costs could reach consumers through meat prices.

drawbacks.text: Compliance and liability costs would fall on large operators, who could pass some of them to consumers through higher meat prices; the bill bars companies from cutting grower payments to cover the new fee but does not control retail prices.

The $750 million grant program is limited to facilities with a labor peace agreement — a pact with a union that recognizes the union if a majority of workers choose it — which steers federal money toward unionized plants and away from non-union ones, whatever one thinks of that trade-off.

The bill gives any person the right to sue operators or USDA over violations, with attorney's fees to prevailing plaintiffs, which could generate litigation reaching beyond the worst practices it targets.

Terminating the New Swine and New Poultry Inspection Systems reverses inspection modernization the industry argues improved efficiency and safety oversight; some processing capacity and speed would be lost, and the shortened transport window (8 hours, replacing the 28-hour rule, for operator shipments) would require significant logistics changes — though that piece does not take effect for 10 years.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits — worker protections, disaster cost-shifting onto the companies that create the risks, and an end to the most painful mass-killing and fastest slaughter-line practices — are real and targeted at practices the bill's own findings say affected over 70 million animals since 2019 and cost taxpayers millions. The costs are borne by the large companies causing the harms, though consumers could see some price increases and the union-conditioned grant money and broad private right of action are fair points of criticism. The bill is aggressive but its costs mostly track the harms it addresses; its main flaw is political, not design — it was so sweeping that it drew no committee action at all.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Cory Booker introduced the bill on February 2, 2023, joined by Senators Elizabeth Warren and Brian Schatz as cosponsors.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry.
No markup, hearing, or floor vote ever followed; the referral was the bill's final action, and it expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large industrial livestock operators and meatpackers came out ahead: they avoided the annual fees, disaster liability, severance and health-coverage mandates, depopulation bans, and the termination of higher-speed slaughter lines, all of which remain in place unchanged.

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and championed it

against.name: Senate Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry Committee
against.role: Senate committee of referral (Chair Debbie Stabenow, D-MI)
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral; no hearing, markup, or vote on the bill ever occurred

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever happened, so no voting split exists; the bill's only support came from three Senate Democrats, and the Democratic-led Agriculture Committee never brought it up, so neither party ever had to take a position.

industries.industry: Industrial livestock operators (large factory farms and CAFOs)
industries.note: Would face registration, annual fees of at least $1 per animal unit, full liability for disaster and depopulation costs including payments to neighboring residents, bans on the cheapest culling methods with penalties up to $1,000 per animal, and a ban on using incarcerated workers. Its cost-shifting onto growers, workers, and neighbors is precisely what the bill targets.

Would lose higher-speed slaughter lines and company-employee self-inspection under the New Swine and New Poultry Inspection Systems, would be barred from slaughtering or selling downed livestock, and poultry would come under humane slaughter law for the first time. Grant money would flow to smaller processors instead, and grant recipients would be barred from merging with packers holding over 10% market share.

Would get a $750 million program to transition to gas-based stunning, a five-year pilot adding free inspections and technical assistance, and research funding — aimed at leveling the field in a market the bill describes as dominated by a few large firms.

industries.industry: Animal drug makers (beta-agonists such as ractopamine, zilpaterol, lubabegron)
industries.note: The bill would prohibit using these growth-promotion and feed-efficiency drugs in healthy animals, eliminating that market segment; the bill ties them to livestock becoming nonambulatory.

Carriers hauling for large operators would face stricter standards — bedding, water, temperature limits, and an 8-hour confinement limit replacing the 28-hour rule — with the harshest parts phased in over a decade.
